newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French December bond futures traded in a narrow range on Monday, taking a breather after last week's rally, to settle little changed despite a U.S. bond slide late in the session.

The contract opened at 124.80 and traded between 124.74 and 124.90 before settling at 124.82. Only 47,346 contracts traded, the lowest volume since September 2 and less than a third of the volume last Friday.
Traders said the main focus for the week remained U.S. jobs figures out on Friday, although European bond markets were relatively immune from U.S. bond weakness on Monday.
French bonds hardly budged when U.S. bonds fell on the back of strong home sales and an increase in the prices paid component of the Chicago purchasing managers index.

A bond analyst in Paris said the increase in the prices paid component was a local problem for the United States and probably reflected firms' attempts to preserve margins in the face of declining capacity utilisation and productivity.

"It's not a worry for Europe, inflation is not at all a European problem. A slight slowdown in the U.S. is provoking a temporary increase in prices but it's a local problem," he said. "I'm not worried by the European reaction to U.S. bonds."
A trader said the market was more interested in the U.S. non-farm payrolls due on Friday and the National Association of Purchasing Management's September report due on Tuesday.

There was little reaction to the French national statistics institutes monthly survey of business leaders. It showed that although the overall outlook remained mediocre, on a personal level the outlook was little changed, and suggested a slight growth in production in the months ahead.
The one-day strike called by French teachers had little impact on the currency. The franc was trading at 3.3832 per mark at 1530 GMT, down slightly from 3.3808 on Friday.

French primary dealers appeared split as to which bonds they expected the Treasury to auction on Thursday. In addition to the October 2006 OAT, some said they would like to see more of the TEC 10 variable rate bond on offer, while others sided firmly with an issue of 2011 paper.
One analyst said the demand for longer-dated paper from French domestic investors, still flush with liquidity and looking for yield, would prompt the Treasury to issue more 2011 OATs.
Others said there was still plenty of demand for the TEC 10, the bond which met with most demand at last month's auction.
The Treasury will announce the lines on offer at Thursday's auction tomorrow morning from 0900 GMT.
The 10-year spread over Bunds narrowed slightly to one basis point from three on Friday.
